core: Working definition of management: coordinating people and resources to reach an organization's goals, based on the attributed OpenStax definition ('the process of guiding the development, maintenance, and allocation of resources to attain organizational goals').
The four functions of management: planning, organizing, leading, and controlling, each with one line and an original example.
The three levels of management: top (executives), middle, and first-line, each named with one line (OpenStax Principles of Management).
What managers do day to day: set goals, assign tasks, review progress, solve problems — the practical list grounded in studies of managerial work.
Management versus leadership: position and process versus influence and direction, stated simply; leadership referenced only as a sibling topic.
Why management matters: without coordination, effort scatters.
Honest framing: management is a skill, not a title.
supporting: Efficiency (least resources for the work) versus effectiveness (producing the desired result); managers need both.
The four functions form a tightly integrated cycle, with managers performing more than one at a time.
Studies of managers in action (Mintzberg, Kotter, Sproull, summarized by OpenStax): constant task-switching, short activities, most time spent with other people.
Running a business involves continuous practical management of finances, employees, taxes, and compliance (SBA business guide).
outOfScope: Leadership depth — owned by the leadership sibling topic.
Organizational structure and design depth — owned by the organizational-structure sibling topic.
Human-resource practices (recruiting, compensation, labor law) — owned by the human-resources sibling topic.
Management history and theory schools (scientific management, human relations, etc.) — beyond this literacy lesson.
Mintzberg's full role typology and strategic planning frameworks — owned by business-strategy territory.

claims.claim: Management is the process of guiding the development, maintenance, and allocation of resources to attain organizational goals; managers are the people responsible for carrying out that process.
The management process rests on four key functional areas: planning, organizing, leading, and controlling, which form a tightly integrated cycle rather than separate steps.

Planning means setting objectives, examining alternatives, determining needed resources, and creating strategies; controlling means measuring performance, comparing it to standards, and taking corrective action.

Organizations have three general levels of management: top managers (executives, responsible for the entire organization and its strategic direction), middle managers (responsible for major departments, may supervise lower-level managers), and first-line managers (supervise rank-and-file employees and carry out day-to-day activities).

Studies of managers in action find that managers switch frequently between tasks, work in many short-duration activities, and spend most of their working time with other people, gathering information, identifying problems, developing plans, and giving direction.

Management and leadership are distinct: management copes with complexity through planning, budgeting, organizing, staffing, and controlling, while leadership copes with change by setting direction, aligning people, and motivating them; strong organizations need both.

Running a business means continuously managing practical areas such as finances, employees, taxes, compliance, assets, and marketing; management is ongoing day-to-day work rather than a one-time event.

Efficiency is using the least possible amount of resources to get work done, while effectiveness is the ability to produce a desired result; managers need to be both efficient and effective to achieve organizational goals.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The names for the three management levels vary across sources (top/middle/first-line versus executive/middle/first-line versus senior/middle/supervisory).
positions: OpenStax Principles of Management names executives, middle management, and first-line management, describing executives as responsible for the entire organization and its strategic direction.
Many business guides and textbooks use top, middle, and first-line as the standard three levels.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses top, middle, and first-line as the primary names, notes that top managers are also called executives, and does not claim the labels are universal.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The boundary between management and leadership is debated: some treatments present leadership as one of the manager's activities, while others treat management and leadership as distinct and complementary.
positions: Kotter (HBR): management copes with complexity, leadership copes with change; both are necessary and complementary.
Textbooks that list leading as one of the four management functions treat leadership as part of management.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both views compatibly: leading is one of the four functions, while the management-versus-leadership distinction follows Kotter's framing, stated simply as position and process versus influence and direction. Depth is deferred to the leadership sibling topic.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). Verified live via HTTP fetch on 2026-08-21. Supports: management as the process of guiding the development, maintenance, and allocation of resources to attain organizational goals; managers as the people responsible for the process; the four key functions (planning, organizing, leading, controlling) as a tightly integrated cycle; the function descriptions (planning: set objectives, examine alternatives, determine resources, create strategies; organizing: design jobs, create structure, staff positions, coordinate work; leading: lead and motivate, communicate, resolve conflicts, manage change; controlling: measure performance, compare to standards, take action); efficiency versus effectiveness; the managerial process as anticipate-design plans, coordinate resources, guide personnel, review results.
